item.title: Gunma Safari Park: A Drive-Through Wildlife Encounter — Guide
item.description: Gunma Safari Park lets visitors experience a drive-through safari within Japan, with lions, tigers, bears and other large animals roaming semi-freely across expansive enclosures that vehicles pass through at a slow, controlled pace. Visitors can drive their own car (following strict safety guidelines) or ride a park safari bus for a more guided experience, while a separate walking zoo section offers closer encounters with smaller animals, feeding experiences, and a petting zone suited to younger children.

item.title: Choshi Whale & Dolphin Watching Guide: Tours & Access
item.description: Few people realise you can go whale and dolphin watching within easy reach of Tokyo — but the rich waters off Choshi, where the warm Kuroshio current meets the cold Oyashio off the Boso Peninsula’s northeastern tip, are one of Japan’s most reliable spots. Boat tours head out from Choshi port to look for large pods of dolphins (often hundreds at a time) and, in season, whales such as minke, Bryde’s and even sperm whales.

item.title: Hokkaido Bear Watching Guide: Where & How to See Brown Bears
item.description: Hokkaido is home to the Ezo brown bear (higuma), Japan’s largest land animal, plus a rich cast of northern wildlife — deer, red foxes, Steller’s sea eagles, red-crowned cranes and whales. Seeing a wild brown bear is a genuine thrill, and Hokkaido offers some of Japan’s best opportunities to do so safely and responsibly, above all from boat cruises along the Shiretoko coast where bears forage on the shore. For guaranteed sightings, well-run bear parks let families get close.

item.title: Sea Turtle Snorkelling Guide: Zamami & Okinawa Tours
item.description: Swimming alongside a wild green sea turtle in Okinawa’s crystal water is a bucket-list moment — and surprisingly attainable. The reefs around Zamami in the Kerama Islands are among the best places in Japan to snorkel with sea turtles, which graze on seagrass close to shore and surface for air right beside swimmers. With easy beach-entry spots and guided tours that know where the turtles feed, it’s an experience open to families and casual snorkellers, not just divers.

item.title: Yanbaru Guide: UNESCO Forest, Wildlife & Access
item.description: The lush, mountainous north of Okinawa Island is Yanbaru — a subtropical forest so biodiverse it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage natural site in 2021. Home to rare endemic creatures found nowhere else on Earth, like the flightless Okinawa rail (Yanbaru kuina) and the Okinawa woodpecker, it offers a completely different Okinawa from the beaches: dense green ridges, waterfalls, mangroves and the dramatic karst formations of Daisekirinzan. It’s the island’s premier destination for nature lovers.

item.title: Jigokudani Snow Monkey Park: Complete Visitor Guide
item.description: Jigokudani Yaen-koen (Hell Valley Wild Monkey Park) is where wild Japanese macaques — the world’s northernmost non-human primates — descend from the surrounding forest to bathe in a natural hot spring pool surrounded by snow. The image is one of the most reproduced photographs of Japan: a red-faced monkey up to its neck in steaming water, eyes half-closed in contentment, snow settling on its dark fur. The reality lives up to the image.
